Succeeded his father Jehoiakin (B.C. 599) when only eight years of age, and reigned for one hundred days (2 Chr. 36:9). He is also called Jeconiah (Jer. 24:1; 27:20, etc.), and Coniah (22:24; 37:1).
ch.s: This chapter covers: Jehoiakim subdued by Nebuchadnezzar (vv. 1–7); Jehoiachim captive in Babylon (vv. 8–20). People named: Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Nebuchadnezzar, Zedekiah, Ammon, Manasseh. Places: Babylon, Jerusalem, Judah, Egypt, Euphrates.
ch.mh: If Jehoiakim had served the Lord, he had not been servant to Nebuchadnezzar.
q: Read verses 1–7 (Jehoiakim subdued by Nebuchadnezzar). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 8–20 (Jehoiachim captive in Babylon), what do you learn about leadership and kingship?
Verse 12 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Jeremiah 52:28. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Jehoiakim’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of family and generations in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of 2 Kings?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: When those intrusted with the counsels of a nation act unwisely, and against their true interest, we ought to notice the displeasure of God in it.
ch.a: Ask God to search your heart, confess what He shows you, and make any right amends.

o: Jerusalem besieged, Zedekiah taken.
The temple burnt, The people carried into captivity.
The rest of the Jews flee into Egypt, Evil-merodach relieves the captivity of Jehoiachin.
bg: The two books of Kings formed originally but one book in the Hebrew Scriptures. The present division into two books was first made by the LXX., which now, with the Vulgate, numbers them as the third and fourth books of Kings, the two books of Samuel being the first and second books of Kings.

Jerusalem, if not actually in the centre of Palestine, was yet virtually so. "It was on the ridge, the broadest and most strongly-marked ridge of the backbone of the complicated hills which extend through the whole country from the plain of Esdraelon to the desert."

Made great by Jehovah. (1.) the son of Jeduthum (1 Chr. 25:3, 9). (2.) The grandfather of the prophet Zephaniah, and the father of Cushi (Zeph. 1:1). (3.) One of the Jewish nobles who conspired against Jeremiah (Jer. 38:1). (4.) The son of Ahikam, and grandson of Shaphan, secretary of king Josiah (Jer. 26:24). After the destruction of Jerusalem (see ZEDEKIAH), Nebuchadnezzar left him to govern the country as tributar
Necho II., the king of Egypt, gained a victory over the Assyrians at Carchemish. (See JOSIAH; MEGIDDO.) This secured to Egypt the possession of the Syrian provinces of Assyria, including Palestine.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Jerusalem besieged, Zedekiah taken (vv. 1–7); The temple burnt, The people carried into captivity (vv. 8–21); The rest of the Jews flee into Egypt, Evil-merodach relieves the captivity of Jehoiachin (vv. 22–30). People named: Gedaliah, Nebuchadnezzar, Zedekiah, Seraiah, Ishmael, Nethaniah. Places: Babylon, Jerusalem, Judah, Riblah, Mizpah.
ch.mh: Jerusalem was so fortified, that it could not be taken till famine rendered the besieged unable to resist.
q: Read verses 1–7 (Jerusalem besieged, Zedekiah taken). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 8–21 (The temple burnt, The people carried into captivity), what do you learn about leadership and kingship?

What does Gedaliah’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
